title: How Flat Should Your Organization Be
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that flattening an organization has real benefits but can be overdone if leaders chase minimal hierarchy as an end in itself. It walks through why fewer layers speeds decisions and closes distance between leadership and frontline staff, then pivots to the downside: without enough structure, decision-making becomes prone to conflict, delay, and paralysis. The author frames the real question not as flat-versus-tall but as how many layers an organization actually needs to produce results efficiently. Mature organizations are urged to periodically audit whether their layers still add value or have become unnecessary cost and drag.
points: Flatter structures speed decisions and shrink the distance between leadership and frontline staff.
Too few layers can concentrate power and leave decisions mired in unresolved conflict.
The right question isn't flat-vs-tall, but how many layers actually add value.
Young organizations and mature ones face opposite versions of the same audit.
quotes: Fewer layers between the CEO and frontline team members have so many benefits that it is reasonable to ask why organizations need layers at all.
The problem with that vision is the nature of people and decision-making. Without the structure of hierarchy, decision-making about anything important becomes rife with conflict and disagreement.
With only two or three layers, decision-making can become too centralized, concentrating too much power in the hands of only a small set of people to control key decisions.
The best organizations figure out how to come together in whatever combination, layering, and centralization are necessary to add the greatest value to the enterprise.
Good leaders don’t deny the need for hierarchy, but neither do they create layers without a strong reason. Unnecessary layers are better for cakes than organizations.
